events.fact: President James Monroe, in his annual message to Congress, set forth the Monroe Doctrine, warning European powers against further colonization or interference in the Americas.
John Brown was hanged at Charles Town, Virginia, for his armed raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, his execution a grim portent of the coming Civil War.

block: On December 2, 1823, President James Monroe laid before Congress the doctrine that bears his name, declaring that the young Republic would brook no fresh European designs upon the soil of the Americas, a steadfast line drawn in defense of liberty's hemisphere. On the same day in 1859, John Brown was hanged at Charles Town for his violent seizure of the arsenal at Harpers Ferry, a deed of bloodshed that hardened the nation toward the great and terrible war soon to come. The Lord governs even the storms men raise against one another, and a Steadfast citizen learns to hold his post in His providence, neither flinching from a righteous duty nor taking up the sword in lawless wrath.

events.fact: President James Monroe signed the act admitting Illinois as the twenty-first state of the Union.
Oberlin Collegiate Institute opened its doors in Ohio, founded by the Rev. John Jay Shipherd and Philo Stewart as a Christian school of learning and labor.

block: On December 3, 1818, President James Monroe signed the act bringing Illinois into the Union as the twenty-first state, extending ordered government across the prairie frontier. On the same day in 1833, the Rev. John Jay Shipherd and Philo Stewart opened Oberlin Collegiate Institute in Ohio, a school founded upon the Gospel and the dignity of honest labor, where the first classes gathered to be shaped in mind and conscience alike. An Upright citizen remembers that knowledge divorced from godliness puffs up, but learning yoked to the fear of the Lord builds men fit to govern themselves and serve their neighbors.

events.fact: The settlers of Berkeley Hundred landed on the James River in Virginia and, by their charter, kept the day as a solemn thanksgiving to Almighty God, the first such observance in English America.
General George Washington bade an emotional farewell to his officers in the Long Room of Fraunces Tavern in New York City as the Continental Army disbanded after the Revolution.

block: On December 4, 1619, the men of Berkeley Hundred came ashore on the James River and obeyed their charter's charge that the day of their arrival be kept perpetually holy as a day of thanksgiving to Almighty God, the first such observance on these shores. On the same day in 1783, General George Washington, his eyes filled with tears, took leave of his faithful officers at Fraunces Tavern in New York, embracing each in turn before laying down his command. Both scenes teach a Steadfast citizen to begin and end every labor upon his knees before the God who grants the victory, giving thanks at the landing and humbly surrendering the sword at the parting.

events.fact: Martin Van Buren, the eighth President of the United States and the first born a citizen of the new Republic, was born at Kinderhook, New York.
The Twenty-first Amendment was ratified when Utah became the thirty-sixth state to approve it, repealing the prohibition of the Eighteenth Amendment.

block: On December 5, 1782, Martin Van Buren was born at Kinderhook, New York, the first man to hold the presidency who had entered the world under the flag of an independent United States rather than as a subject of the Crown. On the same day in 1933, Utah cast the deciding vote ratifying the Twenty-first Amendment, ending the long experiment of national prohibition and returning the matter to the conscience of the several states. A Steadfast citizen marks how a free people governs itself by sober deliberation, holding fast through the seasons when its laws are amended and its leaders pass, for the Republic endures upon the constancy of ordinary men.

events.fact: The Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution was ratified when Georgia became the twenty-seventh state to approve it, abolishing slavery throughout the United States.
The capstone was set atop the Washington Monument in the nation's capital, completing the great obelisk raised in honor of the first President.

block: On December 6, 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment reached the threshold of ratification when Georgia became the twenty-seventh state to approve it, forever abolishing the bondage that had long burdened the Republic's conscience and obeying at last the higher law written upon the heart. On the same day in 1884, workmen set the aluminum capstone atop the Washington Monument, crowning the towering tribute to the father of his country. An Obedient citizen honors both the law that frees and the memory it enshrines, submitting his own will to the commandments of God who calls every nation to do justice and to walk humbly before Him.

events.fact: Delaware became the first state to ratify the United States Constitution, approving it by a unanimous vote of its convention at Dover.

Imperial Japan launched a surprise attack on the United States Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, killing more than two thousand four hundred Americans and drawing the nation into the Second World War.

block: On December 7, 1787, the delegates of Delaware voted unanimously to ratify the new Constitution, earning forever the honor of being the First State to bind itself to the federal compact. On the same day in 1941, Japanese aircraft fell without warning upon the fleet at Pearl Harbor, and more than two thousand four hundred Americans perished in a single morning that summoned a nation to war. From the quiet courage of statesmen to the sudden valor of sailors caught in the fire, an Enduring citizen learns to stand fast in the day of testing, trusting that the God who has carried the Republic through its darkest mornings will not abandon it now.

events.fact: President Abraham Lincoln issued the Proclamation of Amnesty and Reconstruction, offering pardon to those in rebellion who would swear allegiance to the United States.
President Franklin Roosevelt addressed Congress, calling December 7 'a date which will live in infamy,' and the United States declared war on Japan.

block: On December 8, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln issued his Proclamation of Amnesty and Reconstruction, extending the hand of pardon to those who would forsake the rebellion and swear renewed allegiance to the Union, a mercy offered even amid the agony of civil war. On the same day in 1941, President Franklin Roosevelt stood before Congress and named December 7 a date which would live in infamy, and the Republic resolved upon war against Japan. A Steadfast citizen holds firm in the hour of decision as Roosevelt did, yet keeps room in his heart for Lincoln's mercy, for the God he serves is at once a righteous judge and a forgiver of the penitent.

events.fact: Noah Webster established the American Minerva, New York City's first daily newspaper, advancing an informed and virtuous citizenry in the young Republic.
The first Christmas Seals went on sale in Wilmington, Delaware, through the efforts of Emily Bissell, raising funds to fight tuberculosis among the poor.

block: On December 9, 1793, the lexicographer Noah Webster founded the American Minerva, the first daily newspaper in New York City, laboring to furnish a free people with the knowledge and moral instruction a self-governing nation requires. On the same day in 1907, Emily Bissell sold the first Christmas Seals in Wilmington, Delaware, a humble penny stamp that gathered the charity of countless neighbors to relieve the sick and dying of tuberculosis. A Steadfast citizen perseveres in such quiet, faithful work, knowing that the God who multiplied loaves and fishes still uses the small and steady offering of His servants to bless a whole people.

events.fact: President James Madison approved the resolution admitting Indiana as the nineteenth state of the Union.
Germany and Italy declared war on the United States, and Congress answered the same day, committing the Republic fully to the struggle of the Second World War.

block: On December 11, 1816, President James Madison signed the resolution admitting Indiana as the nineteenth state, planting ordered liberty deeper into the western country. On the same day in 1941, Germany and Italy declared war upon the United States, and Congress, undaunted, answered in kind before the sun had set, resolving to see the fight through to the end. A Steadfast citizen meets such a summons without wavering, for he has learned that the God who founds nations also calls them to defend the gift of freedom against every tyrant who would extinguish it.

events.fact: Dartmouth College was chartered in New Hampshire by the Rev. Eleazar Wheelock, established for the instruction of youth in Christian learning.
Union forces under General Burnside hurled themselves against entrenched Confederate lines at Marye's Heights in the Battle of Fredericksburg, Virginia, and were repulsed with grievous loss.

block: On December 13, 1769, the Rev. Eleazar Wheelock received the royal charter for Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, founding a seat of learning to train young men in the knowledge of God and the arts of civilized life. On the same day in 1862, wave upon wave of Union soldiers charged the stone wall at Marye's Heights in Fredericksburg, Virginia, and fell in terrible numbers before the Confederate guns, their courage undimmed by the hopelessness of the assault. A Steadfast citizen honors both the patient labor that builds and the desperate valor that endures, trusting that the God who ordains a nation's trials also redeems the sacrifice of brave men for purposes beyond their sight.

events.fact: George Washington, first President of the United States and commander of the Continental Army, died at his home at Mount Vernon, Virginia.
President James Monroe signed the resolution admitting Alabama as the twenty-second state of the Union.

block: On December 14, 1799, George Washington breathed his last at Mount Vernon, the great soldier and statesman meeting death with the same composure with which he had borne the weight of a nation, commending himself calmly to his Maker. On the same day in 1819, President James Monroe signed the act admitting Alabama as the twenty-second state, the Union still growing even as its founding father was laid to rest. A Steadfast citizen patterns his own life upon Washington's, holding his course faithfully to the end, that he too may surrender his earthly charge in peace and pass into the keeping of the God he served.

events.fact: Virginia became the deciding state to ratify the Bill of Rights, and the first ten amendments to the Constitution took effect, securing the liberties of the American people.
Union forces under General George Thomas opened the Battle of Nashville, Tennessee, shattering General Hood's Confederate Army of Tennessee in a decisive victory.

block: On December 15, 1791, Virginia cast the deciding vote that gave force to the Bill of Rights, enshrining in the Constitution the freedoms of conscience, speech, and worship that no government may rightly take away. On the same day in 1864, General George Thomas loosed his army upon General Hood's forces at Nashville, breaking the Confederate Army of Tennessee in one of the war's most complete victories. A Steadfast citizen guards the liberties his fathers secured and stands firm in the field when they must be defended, knowing that the God who is the author of freedom requires faithful men to keep it.

events.fact: Colonists in Boston, protesting taxation without representation, boarded British ships and cast their cargoes of tea into the harbor in the act remembered as the Boston Tea Party.
German forces launched a massive surprise offensive through the Ardennes forest, beginning the Battle of the Bulge, the last great German assault of the Second World War in the West.

block: On December 16, 1773, the men of Boston, resolved against taxation laid upon them without their consent, boarded three ships in the harbor and heaved their chests of tea into the cold tide, a bold stroke that set the colonies on the road to independence. On the same day in 1944, the Germans hurled their last great offensive through the snowbound Ardennes, and American soldiers, surprised and surrounded, dug in and held until the line was restored at fearful cost. A Steadfast citizen draws strength from both the defiance of Boston harbor and the grit of the Ardennes, trusting that the God who hates injustice steels the hearts of free men to resist the oppressor.

events.fact: The French foreign minister, the Comte de Vergennes, formally announced that France would recognize the independence of the United States, a turning point in the Revolution secured by the victory at Saratoga.
Orville and Wilbur Wright achieved the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered aircraft near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

block: On December 17, 1777, the Comte de Vergennes informed the American envoys that France would recognize the independence of the United States, an alliance won by the blood of Saratoga that would prove decisive in the long fight for liberty. On the same day in 1903, two bicycle makers from Ohio, Orville and Wilbur Wright, lifted their flimsy machine off the sands at Kitty Hawk and held it aloft under a man's control, opening the age of flight by patient labor and dauntless trial. A Steadfast citizen perseveres as the Wrights did through every failure, and waits as the patriots did for help in God's appointed hour, confident that diligence and faith are never finally disappointed.

events.fact: New Jersey became the third state to ratify the United States Constitution, approving it unanimously.
Secretary of State William Seward officially proclaimed the Thirteenth Amendment a part of the Constitution, certifying the abolition of slavery throughout the United States.

block: On December 18, 1787, New Jersey followed close upon her sister states and ratified the Constitution by a unanimous vote, lending her full weight to the new frame of government. On the same day in 1865, Secretary of State William Seward proclaimed to the world that the Thirteenth Amendment had become the supreme law of the land, sealing the abolition of slavery and answering at last the cry that had risen so long against the Republic's great sin. A Steadfast citizen rejoices that God's slow and certain justice cannot be turned aside, and he labors patiently for the right, assured that what is founded upon truth will in time be confirmed and made fast.

events.fact: Thomas Paine's first 'American Crisis' essay appeared, dated December 19, opening with the famous words, 'These are the times that try men's souls.'
General George Washington led the ragged Continental Army into winter quarters at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, to endure a season of bitter cold and want.

block: On December 19, 1776, Thomas Paine's first 'American Crisis' essay went forth with its stirring summons, 'These are the times that try men's souls,' rebuking the summer soldier and the sunshine patriot and calling the wavering to stand. On the same day in 1777, General George Washington marched his hungry and half-clothed army into the frozen camp at Valley Forge, where obedience to duty would be proven not in battle but in patient suffering through a merciless winter. An Obedient citizen learns from Valley Forge that the hardest service is often the quiet endurance of hardship in one's appointed place, holding the line for the cause because the God of hosts has set him there.

events.fact: The Louisiana Territory was formally transferred to the United States in a ceremony at New Orleans, doubling the size of the young Republic through the Louisiana Purchase.
South Carolina became the first state to secede from the Union, an act that opened the way to the Civil War.

block: On December 20, 1803, the flag of the United States rose over New Orleans as France formally surrendered the vast Louisiana country, doubling the nation's domain and entrusting an immense frontier to the stewardship of a free people. On the same day in 1860, South Carolina voted to secede from the Union, the first state to break the bond and the first step down the road to civil war. A Responsible citizen weighs the awful difference between these two days, between a heritage faithfully received and a covenant rashly broken, and resolves to guard the union and liberties God has placed in his trust rather than squander them in passion.

events.fact: The Pilgrims of the Mayflower came ashore at Plymouth, Massachusetts, an event long honored in New England as Forefathers' Day.
General William Tecumseh Sherman's army took the city of Savannah, Georgia, completing the March to the Sea.

block: On December 21, 1620, the Pilgrims stepped ashore at Plymouth after a perilous crossing, a remnant who had crossed an ocean to worship God according to conscience and to plant a godly commonwealth in the wilderness. On the same day in 1864, General Sherman's army marched into Savannah, completing its long campaign across Georgia and hastening the end of the war. A Steadfast citizen looks to the Pilgrims who endured the storm and the killing winter for the sake of their faith, and resolves to hold fast his own profession with the same constancy, come hardship or plenty, by the grace of the God who brought them safely to that rocky shore.

events.fact: The Continental Congress named Esek Hopkins commander in chief of the newly established Continental Navy, the seed of the United States Navy.
Surrounded at Bastogne in the Battle of the Bulge, General Anthony McAuliffe answered a German demand for surrender with a single defiant word: 'Nuts!'

block: On December 22, 1775, the Continental Congress appointed Esek Hopkins to command the fledgling Continental Navy, sending the new nation's first ships to sea against the mightiest fleet on earth. On the same day in 1944, General Anthony McAuliffe and his men, encircled and outnumbered at Bastogne, met the enemy's call for surrender with the immortal reply of 'Nuts!' and held their ground until relief broke through. A Steadfast citizen takes heart from such defiance against long odds, for the God who armed a young Republic against an empire still strengthens the resolute who refuse to yield what is right.

events.fact: General George Washington resigned his commission as commander in chief before the Continental Congress at Annapolis, Maryland, surrendering his power and returning to private life.
The poem 'A Visit from St. Nicholas,' beginning ''Twas the night before Christmas,' was first published anonymously in the Troy Sentinel of New York.

block: On December 23, 1783, General George Washington stood before Congress at Annapolis and resigned his commission, laying down the sword of supreme command to become once more a private citizen, an act of self-restraint that astonished a watching world and set the pattern for republican virtue. On the same day in 1823, the beloved verses of 'A Visit from St. Nicholas' first appeared in the Troy Sentinel, weaving warmth and wonder into the American Christmas. A Steadfast citizen takes Washington as his model, holding power loosely and laying it down faithfully when his duty is done, for the truly great man is the servant who answers to God above every earthly crown.

events.fact: On Christmas night, General George Washington crossed the ice-choked Delaware River with his army to strike the enemy garrison at Trenton, New Jersey.
President Andrew Johnson issued a proclamation granting unconditional pardon and amnesty to all who had participated in the late rebellion.

block: On the night of December 25, 1776, General George Washington led his weary soldiers across the freezing Delaware River through wind and sleet, a desperate Christmas gamble to fall upon the foe at Trenton and rekindle a cause near despair. On the same day in 1868, President Andrew Johnson proclaimed a full and unconditional pardon to all who had joined the rebellion, extending mercy in the hope of binding up the nation's wounds. A Steadfast citizen remembers that the holy night which gave the world its Savior also found Washington pressing on through the storm, and he too presses forward in faith, trusting the God who came at Christmas to crown perseverance with deliverance.

events.fact: Washington's army surprised and routed the Hessian garrison at the Battle of Trenton, New Jersey, taking nearly a thousand prisoners and reviving the patriot cause.
Henry 'Light-Horse Harry' Lee delivered his famous eulogy of George Washington, praising him as 'first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen.'

block: On December 26, 1776, Washington's storm-battered army fell upon the Hessian troops at Trenton, scattering them and seizing nearly a thousand captives, a stunning victory that breathed new life into a flagging Revolution. On the same day in 1799, Henry Lee rose before a grieving nation to eulogize the lately departed Washington as first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen. A Steadfast citizen finds in Trenton the proof that bold faith rewards the persevering, and in Lee's tribute the measure of a life so given to duty that a whole people mourned it, and he resolves to spend his own days as worthily before the God who weighs every man's labor.

events.fact: Residents of Flushing in New Netherland signed the Flushing Remonstrance, petitioning against the ban on Quaker worship and pleading for liberty of conscience, an early American testimony for religious freedom.
Radio City Music Hall opened its doors in New York City, becoming a celebrated showplace of American enterprise and entertainment.

block: On December 27, 1657, some thirty plain townsmen of Flushing signed the Flushing Remonstrance, boldly petitioning Director-General Stuyvesant against his edict forbidding Quaker worship and declaring that conscience must be left free, a noble forerunner of the religious liberty later enshrined in the Bill of Rights. On the same day in 1932, Radio City Music Hall opened in New York, a monument to the energy and craftsmanship of American industry. A Steadfast citizen honors those Flushing farmers who risked the magistrate's wrath to defend freedom of worship, and he stands as firmly in his own day for the right of every man to serve God according to his conscience.

events.fact: President James K. Polk signed the act admitting Iowa as the twenty-ninth state of the Union.
Woodrow Wilson, the twenty-eighth President of the United States, was born in Staunton, Virginia, the son of a Presbyterian minister.

block: On December 28, 1846, President James K. Polk signed the law admitting Iowa as the twenty-ninth state, drawing the rich farmland of the upper Mississippi under the ordered government of the Union. On the same day in 1856, Woodrow Wilson was born in the Presbyterian manse at Staunton, Virginia, reared from infancy in the Scriptures and the disciplines of the faith that would mark his public life. An Obedient citizen sees in the lawful growth of the Republic and in a minister's son shaped by family worship the same lesson, that nations and men alike prosper when they submit themselves to the God who orders all things and rewards the faithful keeping of His commandments.

events.fact: Texas was admitted as the twenty-eighth state of the Union, completing the annexation of the former Republic of Texas.
Andrew Johnson, who would become the seventeenth President of the United States, was born in humble circumstances at Raleigh, North Carolina.

block: On December 29, 1845, the Lone Star Republic furled its own banner and entered the Union as the twenty-eighth state, the vast country of Texas joining its fortunes to those of the United States. On the same day in 1808, Andrew Johnson was born in poverty at Raleigh, North Carolina, a tailor's apprentice who never saw the inside of a schoolhouse yet rose by toil and resolve to the highest office in the land. An Upright citizen learns from both that honest labor and faithful dealing, not high birth, are the true measure of a man, for the God who exalts the lowly looks upon the integrity of the heart.

events.fact: British forces burned the village of Buffalo, New York, to the ground during the War of 1812, in retaliation for the American burning of Newark in Canada.
The Gadsden Purchase treaty was signed at Mexico City, by which the United States acquired the southern lands of present-day Arizona and New Mexico.

block: On December 30, 1813, British troops and their allies put the frontier village of Buffalo to the torch, leaving its hardy settlers homeless in the dead of winter amid the hardships of that frontier war. On the same day in 1853, James Gadsden signed the treaty at Mexico City securing for the United States the desert lands that would round out the southern border of Arizona and New Mexico. A Steadfast citizen recalls how the people of Buffalo rebuilt from the ashes and how a young nation pressed on to settle its frontiers, trusting that the God who sustains a people through fire and loss will yet establish the work of their hands.

events.fact: American forces under General Richard Montgomery and Colonel Benedict Arnold assaulted the fortress city of Quebec and were repulsed, Montgomery falling in the snow at the head of his men.
President Abraham Lincoln signed the act admitting West Virginia to the Union, carving a new loyal state from the mountains of old Virginia.

block: On December 31, 1775, General Richard Montgomery and Colonel Benedict Arnold led a daring assault upon Quebec through a driving snowstorm, only to be thrown back with heavy loss, Montgomery himself struck down at the head of his column in the war's first great defeat. On the same day in 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed the act admitting West Virginia, drawing a new and loyal state from the mountains as the Republic fought for its life. A Steadfast citizen honors the courage that presses an attack against the longest odds and the resolve that builds even in the midst of war, trusting that the God who reigns over victory and defeat alike will carry the faithful through to the end of every year and every trial.
